arXiv:2504.21356v1 [cs.CV] 30 Apr 2025

Nexus-Gen: A Unified Model for Image Understanding, Generation, and Editing

Hong Zhang Affiliation: College of Control Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University Email: {hongzhang99    Zhongjie Duan Affiliation: ModelScope Team, Alibaba Group Inc. East China Normal University Email: zhangyu80}@zju.edu.cn    Xingjun Wang Email: zjduan@stu.ecnu.edu.cn    Yingda Chen Email: 
{xingjun.wxj    Yuze Zhao Email: yingda.chen    Yu Zhang22footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: College of Control Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University Email: yuze.zyz}@alibaba-inc.com
Abstract

Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) aim to integrate multimodal understanding and generation abilities through a single framework. Despite their versatility, existing open-source unified models exhibit performance gaps against domain-specific architectures. To bridge this gap, we present Nexus-Gen, a unified model that synergizes the language reasoning capabilities of LLMs with the image synthesis power of diffusion models. To align the embedding space of the LLM and diffusion model, we conduct a dual-phase alignment training process. (1) The autoregressive LLM learns to predict image embeddings conditioned on multimodal inputs, while (2) the vision decoder is trained to reconstruct high-fidelity images from these embeddings. During training the LLM, we identified a critical discrepancy between the autoregressive paradigm’s training and inference phases, where error accumulation in continuous embedding space severely degrades generation quality. To avoid this issue, we introduce a prefilled autoregression strategy that prefills input sequence with position-embedded special tokens instead of continuous embeddings. Through dual-phase training, Nexus-Gen has developed the integrated capability to comprehensively address the image understanding, generation and editing tasks. All models, datasets, and codes are published on the Project Page to facilitate further advancements across the field.

††footnotetext: Technical report, the project is still in progress at project page

1 Introduction

The emergence of unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has recently sparked considerable interest due to their exceptional proficiency in both understanding and generating cross-modal content. Pioneering closed-source systems such as GPT-4o OpenAI (2025) and Gemini-2.0 Google (2025) Flash exemplify the potential of unified architectures: (1) Enhanced semantic precision: The strong reasoning ability of LLMs significantly enhances precise semantic grounding of generated images. (2) Versatility of tasks: The architectures demonstrate remarkable adaptability in accommodating diverse multimodal tasks including image understanding (Image-to-Text), generation (Text-to-Image), editintg (Image+Text-to-Image), and flexible combinations of these tasks.

The core challenge in transitioning large language models (LLMs) to unified models lies in integrating vision prediction capabilities on the given embedding space Yan et al. (2025). Researchers have extensively explored the unified model and developed open-source frameworks which perform autoregressive prediction of image tokens and decode them via compact image decoders. Chameleon Team (2024), Janus-Pro Chen et al. (2025), and Emu3 Wang et al. (2024) employ a discrete vision embedding space and decode embeddings via VQ tokenizers Sun et al. (2024)). In contrast, Show-O Xie et al. (2024), UniFluid Fan et al. (2025), Harmon Wu et al. (2025), TransFusion Zhou et al. (2025), and MetaMerph Tong et al. (2024b) leverage continuous representations and decode them with VAEs Kingma et al. (2013) or compact diffusion networks Li et al. (2024); Podell et al. (2024). While achieving functional unification of understanding and generation, their image quality or aesthetic score remain inferior to state-of-the-art (SOTA) text-to-image diffusion models. This discrepancy arises from the fact that diffusion models Podell et al. (2024); Esser et al. (2024); Labs (2024) demonstrate superior capabilities in pixel-level image modeling. Furthermore, SOTA diffusion models have undergone extensive pretraining on large-scale datasets and specialized aesthetic preference tuning.

This paper aims to develop a high-performance unified model, Nexus-Gen, for image understanding, generation, and editing, with full open-source release of all methodologies and technical details to promote future advancements in this area. The central idea involves extending a pre-trained LLM by retaining its inherent understanding capabilities while introducing visual token prediction functionality, where predicted visual tokens are directly fed into a powerful diffusion model to ensure high-quality image generation. This paradigm resembles the workflow of GPT-4o: token → [transformer] → [diffusion] → pixels, where tokens are processed by a transformer, transmitted to a diffusion model, and ultimately converted into pixel outputs. As shown in Figure 2, Nexus-Gen processes input images through a vision encoder, and feed them into the autoregressive transformer together with text tokens. The autoregressive transformer generates output visual tokens and transform them into image embeddings via a vision projector and subsequently decode them into images by a powerful diffusion vision decoder. To keep information integrity and ensure embedding versatility cross diverse tasks, we align input and output image embeddings within a shared continuous feature space.

Based on the above architecture, we have further undertaken the following works. First, we identify the issue of error accumulation phenomenon of the continuous image embeddings, which is caused by inconsistencies between training and inference behaviors in the autoregressive paradigm. To address this, we develop the prefilled autoregression strategy, which prefills special learnable image tokens to harmonize training and inference behaviors and eliminates error accumulation. Second, for fused training across image understanding, generation, and editing tasks, we design a unified task representation and subsequently collect and partially re-annotate approximately 20 million samples for subsequent training. Third, we conduct a dual-phase alignment training process. For the autoregressive transformer, we initialize it with Qwen2.5-VL Bai et al. (2025) and conduct three-stage training to progressively equip it with image generation and editing capabilities. For the vision decoder, we fine-tune it to reconstruct high-fidelity images from the shared embedding space. Finally, through case studies of Nexus-Gen, we validate its capabilities in image understanding, generation, and editing tasks.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We propose Nexus-Gen, a unified model architecture that achieves universal capabilities in image understanding, generation, and editing through the design of a universal task representation, construction of large-scale datasets, and dual-phase supervised fine-tuning.

  • •

    To address error accumulation in continuous image embeddings under autoregressive paradigm, we introduce the prefilled autoregression strategy, which unifies computational behavior of image tokens during training and inference phases, eliminating cumulative errors.

  • •

    We validate the model’s capabilities in image understanding, generation, and editing. All training data, model weights, and codes for Nexus-Gen are published to promote future advancements in this area.

2 Approach

2.1 Architecture

Nexus-Gen adopts a unified framework for image understanding, generation and editing, as illustrated in Figure 2. Textual inputs are tokenized by the text tokenizer and projected into text embeddings, while visual inputs are encoded into image embeddings through the vision transformer encoder. These text and image embeddings are jointly fed into an autoregressive transformer to predict the embeddings of output tokens. For the image embeddings generated by the autoregressive transformer, we employ a vision projector to map them into the same feature space as the input image embeddings. This design facilitates mutual enhancement between the model’s visual understanding and generation capabilities and promotes task extensibility. For instance, the generated image embeddings can be directly fed back into the model itself for advanced image understanding, editing, or even enabling image-generation-based multi-step reasoning. The text embeddings produced by the autoregressive transformer are converted into logits by the text projector, culminating in token ID classification. In our architecture, the vision encoder, autoregressive transformer, and text projector are initialized from the vision tower, language model, and language projector of Qwen2.5-VL-7B Instruct Bai et al. (2025), respectively. The vision encoder remains frozen during subsequent training, while the vision projector is designed to a randomly initialized linear layer.

To improve image generation quality, we employ a powerful diffusion model as the vision decoder for pixel-level image modeling. Specifically, we perform full-parameter fine-tuning on the diffusion transformer of FLUX-1.dev Labs (2024), replacing its T5 Raffel et al. (2020) text embeddings with image embeddings as conditional inputs to enable high-quality image reconstruction. To enable the diffusion transformer to process image embeddings, we use a two-layer projector that maps the feature dimension from 3,584 to 4,096.

2.2 Unified Task Representation

Our objective is to unify image understanding, generation, and editing tasks into a cohesive framework that allows any-to-any modality operations. Thus, we establish a unified task representation for these tasks, which is illustrated as follows. We employs <image> as a placeholder for input or output images. In this unified representation, user-provided messages may consist exclusively of text or a combination of text and images. Similarly, the model (assistant) can generate outputs in either or both modalities: for text, it outputs token IDs; for images, it produces embeddings. Example structures for image understanding, generation, and editing tasks are demonstrated below. With this standardized format established, all subsequent dataset curation processes strictly adhere to this unified representation schema.

During model training, each sample’s messages are formatted into a sequence according to the chat template. When training on this sequence, loss is computed exclusively for tokens associated with the assistant role, encompassing both text and image modalities. For text tokens, we apply cross-entropy loss for token id classification. For image embeddings , we employ a hybrid loss combining mean squared error and cosine similarity loss to supervise regression. Empirically, we observe that MSE loss enforces pixel-level fidelity by penalizing deviations in fine-grained details, while cosine similarity loss prioritizes semantic alignment by optimizing directional coherence in the embedding space. To balance detail preservation and semantic consistency, we jointly optimize both losses. The composite loss function is formulated as:

L=λ1⋅LC​E+λ2⋅LM​S​E+λ3⋅LC​O​SL=\lambda_{1}\cdot L_{CE}+\lambda_{2}\cdot L_{MSE}+\lambda_{3}\cdot L_{COS} (1)

where λ1=0.1\lambda_{1}=0.1, λ2=0.5\lambda_{2}=0.5, λ3=0.5\lambda_{3}=0.5 are hyperparameters that controlling loss weights.

2.3 Prefilled Autoregression

In practice, significant error accumulation phenomenon is observed in the continuous feature space of image embeddings, which is caused by the inconsistency between the training and inference behaviors of autoregressive models. As illustrated in Figure 3, during training, each token in the sequence is predicted based on the ground truth of its preceding tokens. In contrast, in test time, the preceding tokens are generated autoregressively. For discrete text tokens, the model first predicts the token index through classification and then retrieves the corresponding ground truth embedding for input. Therefore, when classification accuracy remains consistently high, the system can effectively mitigate error accumulation. In contrast, when processing continuous image embeddings, the model directly predicts the embedding and feeds it back into the input. This introduces prediction errors into the input, causing progressively larger errors for subsequent tokens. The per-token loss curve during train and test time is shown in Figure 4, where test loss is significantly larger than train loss.

Prior research Li et al. (2024) has shown that image token prediction can be performed in any order, such as raster or random order. Based on this, we can make the following assumption: the embedding of each image token can be directly computed using the text caption and the positional encoding, without relying on preceding image embeddings. In other words, the input sequence does not require the ground truth of image embeddings. Therefore, we propose a strategy called prefilled autoregression to address the issue of error accumulation. which is shwon in illustrated in Figure 3. During training, we utilize a learnable special image token as the prefilled embedding for all image tokens. During inference, since the number of image tokens is fixed, once the BOI token is predicted, we can directly prefill the input sequence with N special image tokens, ensuring consistent behavior compared with training. Under this strategy, the error-affected image embeddings predicted by the model are not fed back to the input sequence, thereby avoiding error accumulation.

By adopting the prefilled autoregression strategy, we successfully eliminate the error accumulation. Under the same experimental conditions, the mean squared error for image embeddings during inference significantly decrease compared to naive autoregression, as shown in Figure 5.

2.4 Dataset Curation

To enable Nexus-Gen with unified visual capabilities, it is necessary to collect datasets for image understanding, generation, and editing, and transform them into the unified task representation. The majority of our dataset derives from publicly accessible open-source repositories. Furthermore, we will release all collected training data that has undergone unified format conversion.

Image Understanding

This task is structured with multimodal inputs (image-text pairs) and text-only outputs, which serves as a direct indicator of model’s chat and understanding ability. While MLLMs inherently possess such cross-modal reasoning capabilities, this task is still critical during training to prevent capacity degradation. We adopt Cambrian-7M Tong et al. (2024a) as the data source, a comprehensive dataset spanning multiple domains including optical character recognition, general visual question answering, language, counting, code, math and science tasks. To improve data quality, we reannotate the answers for all samples with Qwen2.5-VL Bai et al. (2025).

Image Generation

The input for this task is the textual description, and the output is an image. Our data sources comprise Journey DB Pan et al. (2023), AnyWord Tuo et al. (2023), Laion-High-Resolution LAION (2024), EliGen TrainSet Zhang et al. (2025), FLUX-Aes gogoduan (2025), and FLUX-T2I jackyhate (2024). With the exception of Journey DB and AnyWord, which include image captions, the remaining data sources solely consist of image data. Thus, we employed Qwen2.5-VL Bai et al. (2025) to generate corresponding textual descriptions for these image-only datasets.

Image Editing

The input consists of an image and its corresponding editing instruction, and the output denotes the edited image. Our data sources encompass datasets such as HQ-Edit Hui et al. (2024), UltraEdit Zhao et al. (2024), OmniEdit Wei et al. (2024), StyleBooth Han et al. (2024), and the ImagePulse modelscope (2025) dataset, covering a comprehensive range of editing operations including object modification, object addition, object removal, color alteration and style transfer, etc.

2.5 Training Details

In the design of Nexus-Gen, the output feature space of autoregressive transformer aligns with the input feature space of the vision decoder, enabling us to train them separately. All training hyperparameters are listed in Table 1.

For the transformer, we utilize a three-stage training to progressively augment its image generation and editing capabilities. In the first stage, the model is primarily trained to enhance its image generation ability using a dataset comprising 0.7 million understanding data and 5.3 million generation data. During the second stage, the model is further trained to incorporate image editing functionality, leveraging 2 million understanding data, 5.4 million generation data, and 5.5 million editing data. After completing these two stages, the model has demonstrated robust performance across all three tasks. Finally, a third stage of high-quality supervised fine-tuning is conducted using 2.5 million understanding data, 1.6 million generation data, and 0.9 million editing. Notably, the images generation and editing datasets in stage 3 are all derived from high-quality data sources by FLUX-1.dev.

The training objective of the powerful diffusion vision decoder is to align its input feature space with the output feature space of the vision encoder. This is achieved by reconstructing high-quality images from image embeddings encoded by the vision encoder, with the training loss defined as the standard diffusion loss of rectified flow Esser et al. (2024). The training dataset comprises 2 million high-quality images.

3 Case Studies

Nexus-Gen demonstrates proficiency in executing image understanding, generation, and editing tasks. Beyond individual task execution, it supports synergistic task integration to achieve enhanced outcomes. For instance, its linguistic capabilities can be used to polish the image descriptions, thereby facilitating higher-quality image synthesis. Nexus-Gen further allows for iterative refinement of image generation and optimization through conversational feedback loops.

3.1 Image Understanding

As illustrated in Figure 6, Nexus-Gen exhibits comprehensive multimodal image understanding capabilities, including but not limited to visual captioning, optical character recognition, general visual question answering, mathematical problem solving, etc. Furthermore, the joint training framework integrating both understanding and generation objectives enables the model to develop enhanced capabilities in fine-grained visual comprehension.

3.2 Image Generation

Figure 7 showcases representative high-fidelity images synthesized by Nexus-Gen, demonstrating the model’s capability to accurately interpret semantic information from textual descriptions and translate them into visually coherent outputs.

Furthermore, as demonstrated in Figure 8, Nexus-Gen leverages its multimodal language understanding to enhance visual synthesis through a two-stage generation process. When processing underspecified textual prompts, the model systematically enriches the input queries with spatial relationships, material properties, and contextual logic and then translate these refined textual prompts into visual outputs. This showcases the model’s potential in reasoning-driven image synthesis.

3.3 Image Editing

The image editing capabilities of Nexus-Gen are showcased in Figure 9. It seamlessly handles a broad spectrum of editing workflows—from color adjustments and object manipulation to element addition/removal and style transfer. Leveraging its advanced generative capabilities, Nexus-Gen further excels at intricate tasks, such as multi-instruction hybrid editing and story-driven modifications.
